articleSections.heading: Why Fad Diets Fail
articleSections.body: Restrictive diets trigger metabolic adaptation - your body burns fewer calories at rest. When you return to normal eating, weight comes back. A dietitian works with your metabolism, not against it.

articleSections.heading: Your Personalised Nutrition Plan
articleSections.body: Your plan is built around your actual life: foods available in your area, cooking skills, budget, cultural preferences, and family needs. No expensive supplements or hard-to-find ingredients.

articleSections.heading: Realistic Weight Loss Targets
articleSections.body: Healthy loss is 0.5-1 kg per week. Faster loss means water and muscle, not fat. Your dietitian tracks more than the scale: measurements, energy levels, blood work, and how your clothes fit.

articleSections.heading: Emotional Eating and Habits
articleSections.body: Most overeating is not about hunger. It is triggered by stress, boredom, loneliness, or habit. A dietitian helps you identify triggers and build alternative responses - the skill that keeps weight off permanently.

articleSections.heading: Support Between Sessions
articleSections.body: Message your dietitian between appointments for quick questions, meal photo reviews, and accountability check-ins. This continuity makes the difference between regaining and maintaining.

title: Eating Well with Diabetes: Blood Sugar Control Through Smart Nutrition
subtitle: South Africa has the highest diabetes rate in Africa - but diet can turn it around
author: Bouul Health Services Team
problemHeadline: Why medication alone is never enough
problemBody: South Africa faces a diabetes epidemic with over 4.5 million diagnosed adults. While medication manages blood sugar acutely, nutrition is the foundation. Carb counting, GI awareness, meal timing, and portion control directly affect HbA1c. A dietitian helps you design a meal pattern that stabilises blood sugar without feeling deprived.

aiPromptExample: I was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 6 months ago. My HbA1c is 9.2 despite metformin. Can a dietitian really help lower this?
aiDiagnosisOutput: HbA1c of 9.2% (average glucose 11.5 mmol/L) is well above the target of 7%. Yes, dietitian intervention can make a significant difference. The approach is to distribute carbohydrates evenly, pair them with protein and fibre, choose low-GI SA staples (sweet potato, samp, whole-grain pap), and time meals consistently with medication.

articleSections.heading: Understanding Carbohydrates
articleSections.body: Carbs have the biggest impact on blood sugar but are not the enemy. Your dietitian teaches you carb counting and choosing the right carbs from everyday SA foods: samp, beans, whole grains, and vegetables.

articleSections.heading: Building Your Plate
articleSections.body: The plate method: fill half with non-starchy veg, quarter with lean protein, quarter with carbs. This simple visual works for any cuisine.

articleSections.heading: Reading Food Labels
articleSections.body: Learn to spot hidden sugars (dextrose, maltose, fruit juice concentrate) and understand serving sizes. Most people are shocked by how much sugar is in common supermarket items.

articleSections.heading: Eating Out and Social Events
articleSections.body: Diabetes does not mean no braais or celebrations. Learn which dishes to prioritise, portion estimation, and how to manage alcohol (which can cause delayed hypoglycaemia).

articleSections.heading: Monitoring and Adjusting
articleSections.body: Pattern management - looking at blood glucose readings over time to identify what works. CGMs are increasingly available in SA and provide real-time feedback.

aiPromptExample: I am training for the Comrades Marathon. I hit a wall around 50 km in long runs. What am I missing nutritionally?
aiDiagnosisOutput: Hitting the wall at 50 km indicates inadequate carbohydrate availability. You need 60-90 g of carbohydrate per hour during the event starting from hour 1. Specific adjustments: periodised carb loading 48 hrs before long runs, practicing race-day nutrition in training, and post-run protein within 30 minutes.

articleSections.heading: Pre-Training Fuel
articleSections.body: Eat 2-3 hours before training: carb-rich, moderate protein, low fibre and fat. SA options: oats with banana, peanut butter toast, or a maas smoothie.

articleSections.heading: During-Exercise Nutrition
articleSections.body: For sessions over 60 min, 30-60g carb per hour. Practice your nutrition strategy in training, not on race day. Gels, sports drinks, or real food - whatever works for your gut.

articleSections.heading: Recovery Nutrition
articleSections.body: The 30-minute window post-training is when muscles are most receptive. Aim for 3:1 or 4:1 carb-to-protein ratio. A post-training snack improves recovery dramatically.

articleSections.heading: Hydration in the SA Climate
articleSections.body: South Africa heat accelerates fluid loss. Weigh before and after training to determine sweat rate. Replace 125-150% of losses within 2 hours. Electrolytes essential for sessions over 90 min.

articleSections.heading: Supplements That Work
articleSections.body: Creatine monohydrate, caffeine, beta-alanine, and carb-electrolyte drinks have strong evidence. Your dietitian advises what is appropriate for your goals, saving money on products that do not deliver.

articleSections.heading: Understanding Your Gut Microbiome
articleSections.body: Your gut contains trillions of bacteria affecting digestion, immunity, mood, and weight. Diet is the single biggest factor shaping your microbiome. Processed foods, low fibre, and artificial sweeteners disrupt the balance.

articleSections.heading: Common Triggers in the SA Diet
articleSections.body: Refined maize meal, white bread, high-sugar cereals, and processed meats can be problematic. But triggers are highly individual.

articleSections.heading: The FODMAP Approach
articleSections.body: FODMAPs are fermentable carbs causing gas and bloating in sensitive people. A low-FODMAP diet temporarily removes high-FODMAP foods, then systematically reintroduces them as a diagnostic tool.

articleSections.heading: Probiotics and Prebiotics
articleSections.body: Probiotics introduce beneficial bacteria. Prebiotics (fibre that feeds good bacteria) are equally important. Fermented SA foods like maas are natural probiotics.

articleSections.heading: Long-Term Gut Maintenance
articleSections.body: The goal is a diverse, fibre-rich diet nourishing your microbiome. Different plant foods feed different bacteria species. Variety is key.

title: Eating for Two: Essential Nutrition Guidance for a Healthy Pregnancy
subtitle: What you eat during pregnancy shapes your baby's health for life
author: Bouul Health Services Team
problemHeadline: Why eating for two is the wrong advice
problemBody: The old advice of eating for two is not just outdated - it is harmful. Calorie needs increase only modestly (about 300 extra calories in the third trimester), but nutrient needs increase significantly. Folate, iron, calcium, iodine, and DHA all play critical roles in fetal development. A dietitian helps you meet your increased nutrient needs without excessive weight gain, manages pregnancy symptoms through diet, and addresses conditions like gestational diabetes and anaemia common in South African pregnancies.

aiPromptExample: I am 14 weeks pregnant and feel nauseous all day. I am struggling to eat vegetables and worry my baby is not getting enough nutrients. What should I do?
aiDiagnosisOutput: First-trimester nausea (hyperemesis in severe cases) is extremely common and does not typically harm the baby - your body has nutrient stores. The priority is eating what you can tolerate. Small, frequent meals (every 2-3 hours), ginger tea, vitamin B6 (25mg 3x daily), and eating a dry cracker before getting out of bed can help. Prenatal vitamins fill gaps. Your dietitian can help you find nutrient-dense foods that do not trigger nausea.

articleSections.heading: Key Nutrients in Pregnancy
articleSections.body: Folate (400-800 mcg) prevents neural tube defects. Iron requirements double - 27mg daily. Calcium (1000mg) supports baby bone development. Iodine (220mcg) is critical for brain development. DHA (200mg) supports eye and brain development. Prenatal supplements should cover these basics.

articleSections.heading: Managing Common Symptoms
articleSections.body: Nausea: small frequent meals, ginger, B6. Heartburn: avoid lying down after eating, smaller meals, identify trigger foods. Constipation: increase fibre (fruits, vegetables, whole grains) and water. This is very common in SA pregnancies.

articleSections.heading: Weight Gain Guidelines
articleSections.body: Recommended gain depends on pre-pregnancy BMI. Normal weight: 11.5-16 kg. Overweight: 7-11.5 kg. Obese: 5-9 kg. Excessive gain increases risks of gestational diabetes, large baby, and C-section. Inadequate gain increases risk of low birth weight.

articleSections.heading: Gestational Diabetes
articleSections.body: GDM affects up to 15% of SA pregnancies. Risk factors: family history, previous GDM, BMI over 30, previous large baby. Management: blood glucose monitoring, carbohydrate-controlled diet, exercise. Most cases resolve after delivery but increase future type 2 diabetes risk.

articleSections.heading: Postnatal Nutrition
articleSections.body: Your nutritional needs remain high during breastfeeding (additional 500 calories/day). Continue prenatal vitamins. Iron stores need replenishing if you lost blood during delivery. Your dietitian can help with postnatal weight loss without compromising milk supply.
